questions.title: Regions, Availability Zones, edge locations
questions.short_md:
- **Region** — a geographic area (e.g., `ap-south-1` Mumbai) with independent services, data stays there unless you move it. Choose by latency, data residency/compliance, service availability, cost.
- **Availability Zone** — one or more physically separate data centres in a region with independent power/network, low-latency links. **Deploy across ≥2 AZs for high availability.**
- **Edge locations** — CloudFront/Route 53/WAF points of presence close to users. (Also Local Zones, Wavelength, Outposts for special cases.)
questions.body_md:

questions.title: Shared responsibility model
questions.short_md: AWS secures **"of" the cloud** (hardware, facilities, hypervisor, managed service internals). You secure **"in" the cloud** (IAM, data, encryption choices, network config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The split shifts with service type: on EC2 you patch the OS; on Lambda/Fargate AWS does; on AgentCore/Bedrock you still own prompts, tool permissions and data handling.

questions.title: Account structure
questions.short_md: Use **AWS Organizations** with multiple accounts (dev/staging/prod, security, logging) for blast-radius isolation, separate billing, and **SCP** guardrails. Humans log in via **IAM Identity Center** (SSO) with permission sets, not IAM users.

questions.title: VPC, subnets, route tables
questions.short_md:
- **VPC** — your private network in a region with a CIDR block (e.g., `10.0.0.0/16` = 65,536 addresses).
- **Subnet** — a slice of the VPC CIDR **in one AZ** (`10.0.1.0/24`). AWS reserves 5 IPs per subnet.
- **Route table** — rules deciding where traffic goes; each subnet is associated with one.
- A subnet is **public** if its route table sends `0.0.0.0/0` to an **Internet Gateway**; **private** otherwise.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:**
- **VPC** — your private network in a region with a CIDR block (e.g., `10.0.0.0/16` = 65,536 addresses).
- **Subnet** — a slice of the VPC CIDR **in one AZ** (`10.0.1.0/24`). AWS reserves 5 IPs per subnet.
- **Route table** — rules deciding where traffic goes; each subnet is associated with one.
- A subnet is **public** if its route table sends `0.0.0.0/0` to an **Internet Gateway**; **private** otherwise.

```
 Public subnet route table          Private subnet route table
 10.0.0.0/16 → local                10.0.0.0/16 → local
 0.0.0.0/0   → igw-123              0.0.0.0/0   → nat-abc  (outbound only)
                                    pl-s3       → vpce-s3  (S3 gateway endpoint)
```

questions.title: Internet Gateway vs NAT Gateway
questions.short_md: **IGW** allows two-way internet access for resources with public IPs in public subnets. **NAT Gateway** (placed in a public subnet) lets **private** resources make **outbound** connections (download packages, call external APIs) without being reachable from the internet.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** **IGW** allows two-way internet access for resources with public IPs in public subnets. **NAT Gateway** (placed in a public subnet) lets **private** resources make **outbound** connections (download packages, call external APIs) without being reachable from the internet.

**Cost/design notes:** NAT GW charges per hour **and per GB processed** — high-volume traffic to S3/ECR through NAT gets expensive → use **VPC endpoints**. Use one NAT per AZ for resilience (a single NAT is an AZ single point of failure and adds cross-AZ data charges).

questions.title: Security groups vs Network ACLs
questions.short_md: **Best practice — SG referencing:**
questions.body_md:
| | Security Group | Network ACL |
|---|---|---|
| Attached to | ENI (instance, task, Lambda in VPC, RDS…) | subnet |
| Stateful? | **Stateful** — return traffic automatically allowed | **Stateless** — must allow return (ephemeral ports) |
| Rules | allow only | allow **and deny**, numbered order |
| Typical use | primary firewall, reference other SGs | coarse subnet guardrails, block IP ranges |

**Best practice — SG referencing:**
```
 alb-sg:  inbound 443 from 0.0.0.0/0
 app-sg:  inbound 8000 from alb-sg        ← only the ALB can reach tasks
 db-sg:   inbound 5432 from app-sg        ← only app tasks reach the DB
```

questions.title: Public vs private connectivity — and how private resources reach AWS services
questions.short_md: Private subnets have no inbound internet. To call AWS APIs (S3, ECR, Secrets Manager, Bedrock) from them: via **NAT** (traffic goes out to public endpoints) or via **VPC endpoints** (traffic stays on the AWS network, no NAT needed, can be restricted with endpoint policies).

questions.title: VPC endpoints and PrivateLink
questions.short_md: **Endpoint policies** restrict what can be done through the endpoint (e.g., only your org's buckets) — a data-exfiltration control.
questions.body_md:
| Type | Services | How |
|---|---|---|
| **Gateway endpoint** | **S3, DynamoDB** only | route table entry; **free** |
| **Interface endpoint (PrivateLink)** | most services (ECR, Secrets Manager, STS, Bedrock, CloudWatch Logs, SQS…) | ENI with private IP in your subnet; hourly + per-GB cost; private DNS |
| **PrivateLink endpoint service** | your own service behind an NLB | expose privately to other VPCs/accounts |

**Endpoint policies** restrict what can be done through the endpoint (e.g., only your org's buckets) — a data-exfiltration control.

**ECS in private subnet without NAT needs:** `ecr.api`, `ecr.dkr`, **S3 gateway** (image layers), `logs`, plus `secretsmanager`/`ssm` if used.

questions.title: Connecting VPCs and on-premises
questions.short_md:
| Option | Use |
|---|---|
| **VPC peering** | 1:1 between two VPCs; non-transitive; no overlapping CIDRs |
| **Transit Gateway** | hub-and-spoke for many VPCs + VPN/Direct Connect; transitive routing |
| **Site-to-Site VPN** | encrypted tunnel over internet to on-prem |
| **Direct Connect** | dedicated private line; consistent latency |
| **PrivateLink** | expose a specific service, not whole networks; overlapping CIDRs OK |
| **VPC Lattice** | service-to-service connectivity + auth across VPCs/accounts |

questions.title: CIDR planning
questions.short_md: Plan non-overlapping ranges across VPCs/accounts/on-prem (peering/TGW need it). Leave room: e.g., `/16` per VPC, `/20`–`/22` per subnet (ECS awsvpc and Lambda ENIs consume IPs). Use IPAM for organisation-wide allocation.

questions.title: ENIs and why IP exhaustion happens
questions.short_md: Every ECS task (awsvpc), Lambda-in-VPC hyperplane ENI, RDS, ALB node, interface endpoint uses IPs. Small subnets run out → tasks fail to start ("insufficient free addresses"). Size subnets generously.

questions.title: Authentication vs authorisation in IAM
questions.short_md: **Authentication** — proving who you are (SSO login, access keys, role session, SigV4-signed request). **Authorisation** — deciding whether that principal may do this **action** on this **resource** under these **conditions** (policy evaluation).
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** **Authentication** — proving who you are (SSO login, access keys, role session, SigV4-signed request). **Authorisation** — deciding whether that principal may do this **action** on this **resource** under these **conditions** (policy evaluation).

**IAM identities:** users (avoid for humans/apps), groups, **roles** (assumed temporarily — preferred), federated identities (Identity Center, OIDC like GitLab, SAML).

questions.title: Anatomy of a policy
questions.short_md: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Sid": "ReadTenantDocs", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-docs/tenants/t-42/*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalTag/team": "payments" }, "Bool": { "aws:SecureTransport": "true" } } }] }

questions.title: Policy types and how evaluation works
questions.short_md: **Evaluation logic (simplified):**
questions.body_md:
| Policy type | Attached to | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Identity-based** | user/group/role | what this principal can do |
| **Resource-based** | resource (S3 bucket policy, KMS key policy, SQS, Lambda) | who can access this resource (incl. cross-account) |
| **Trust policy** | role | who may assume the role |
| **Permissions boundary** | user/role | **maximum** permissions the identity-based policy can grant |
| **SCP / RCP** (Organizations) | account/OU | **maximum** for all principals / resources in the account |
| **Session policy** | AssumeRole call | further restrict a session |

**Evaluation logic (simplified):**
```
 1. Explicit DENY anywhere?                      → DENY
 2. SCP / RCP / boundary / session policy allow it? (all applicable must allow) → else DENY
 3. Identity policy OR resource policy allows it? → ALLOW   (same account)
    Cross-account: BOTH the caller's identity policy AND the resource policy must allow
 4. Otherwise                                     → implicit DENY (default)
```
KMS is special: the **key policy** must allow use (identity policies alone aren't enough unless the key policy delegates to IAM).

questions.title: STS AssumeRole and temporary credentials
questions.short_md: A principal calls `sts:AssumeRole` (or `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` for OIDC, `AssumeRoleWithSAML`) and receives **temporary credentials** (access key + secret + session token, expiring in 15 min–12 h). Prefer them over long-lived access keys: auto-expiry, no secret rotation, clear audit trail (CloudTrail shows role session name).
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** A principal calls `sts:AssumeRole` (or `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` for OIDC, `AssumeRoleWithSAML`) and receives **temporary credentials** (access key + secret + session token, expiring in 15 min–12 h). Prefer them over long-lived access keys: auto-expiry, no secret rotation, clear audit trail (CloudTrail shows role session name).

```
 ECS task ──(task role via container credentials endpoint)──► temp creds ──► S3
 GitLab job ──(OIDC JWT)──► AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity ──► temp creds ──► deploy
 Account A role ──AssumeRole──► Account B role (trust policy allows A) ──► B resources
```

questions.title: Least privilege — how do you achieve it in practice?
questions.short_md: Start from specific actions and resource ARNs; use conditions (tags, VPC endpoint, source account); separate roles per service/tool; **IAM Access Analyzer** to generate policies from CloudTrail activity and find unused permissions/external access; review regularly; permission boundaries for delegated role creation.
questions.body_md:
Start from specific actions and resource ARNs; use conditions (tags, VPC endpoint, source account); separate roles per service/tool; **IAM Access Analyzer** to generate policies from CloudTrail activity and find unused permissions/external access; review regularly; permission boundaries for delegated role creation.

**Example — many agent tools on ECS:** give each tool its own task role (or Lambda role) scoped to its resources, rather than one "agent role" with `s3:*`, `dynamodb:*`.

questions.title: Cross-account access patterns
questions.short_md: 1. **Role assumption:** account B has a role trusting account A's role; A assumes it (most common). 2. **Resource policy:** S3/KMS/SQS policy grants account A's principal (both sides must allow). 3. Use `aws:PrincipalOrgID` conditions to allow only your organisation; `sts:ExternalId` for third parties (confused-deputy protection).

questions.title: ABAC (attribute-based access control)
questions.short_md: Grant access based on **tags**: `"Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:ResourceTag/project": "${aws:PrincipalTag/project}"}}` → one policy scales to many teams/projects without editing per resource.

questions.title: KMS and envelope encryption
questions.short_md: KMS manages keys (KMS keys never leave the HSMs unencrypted). **Envelope encryption:** KMS generates a **data key**; you encrypt data locally with the data key, and store the data key **encrypted by the KMS key** next to the data. To decrypt, call KMS to decrypt the data key.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** KMS manages keys (KMS keys never leave the HSMs unencrypted). **Envelope encryption:** KMS generates a **data key**; you encrypt data locally with the data key, and store the data key **encrypted by the KMS key** next to the data. To decrypt, call KMS to decrypt the data key.

```
 GenerateDataKey(KMS key) → { plaintext data key, encrypted data key }
 encrypt file with plaintext key (AES-256) → discard plaintext key
 store: [ciphertext file] + [encrypted data key]
 decrypt: KMS.Decrypt(encrypted data key) → plaintext key → decrypt file
```
Why: large data never goes to KMS, fewer KMS calls, access controlled by key policy + CloudTrail-audited. S3/EBS/RDS/Secrets Manager do this for you with SSE-KMS. AWS-managed vs **customer-managed keys** (control key policy, rotation, cross-account).

questions.title: ALB vs NLB vs Gateway LB
questions.short_md: **ALB concepts:** listener (port/protocol) → rules → **target group** (instances/IPs/Lambda) with health checks; idle timeout (default 60 s — matters for SSE/long requests).
questions.body_md:
| | **ALB** (Layer 7) | **NLB** (Layer 4) | GWLB |
|---|---|---|---|
| Protocols | HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC, WebSocket | TCP, UDP, TLS | IP (GENEVE) |
| Routing | path/host/header/query rules | port-based | to appliances |
| Features | TLS termination, auth (OIDC/Cognito), WAF, sticky sessions | static IPs/Elastic IPs, extreme throughput, preserve source IP, PrivateLink | firewalls/IDS inline |
| Use | web APIs, microservices, ECS | non-HTTP, ultra-low latency, PrivateLink service | security appliances |

**ALB concepts:** listener (port/protocol) → rules → **target group** (instances/IPs/Lambda) with health checks; idle timeout (default 60 s — matters for SSE/long requests).

questions.title: API Gateway vs ALB
questions.short_md: Agent streaming (SSE for minutes) usually fits ALB → ECS, or API Gateway REST response streaming where supported.
questions.body_md:
| | API Gateway (REST/HTTP API) | ALB |
|---|---|---|
| Pricing | per request | per hour + LCU |
| Features | auth (JWT/Cognito/IAM/Lambda authorizers), throttling, usage plans/API keys, request validation, caching (REST), direct service integrations | routing to long-running services, WebSockets, gRPC |
| Limits | **29 s integration timeout** default (can be raised for REST regional/private APIs; HTTP APIs max 30 s), 10 MB payload | long timeouts, large payloads |
| Best for | serverless (Lambda) APIs, public APIs needing throttling/keys | containers/EC2, streaming, high steady traffic |

Agent streaming (SSE for minutes) usually fits ALB → ECS, or API Gateway REST response streaming where supported.

questions.title: Route 53, TLS and certificates
questions.short_md: Route 53: domains + DNS (public/private hosted zones), **alias records** to ALB/CloudFront (free, zone apex), routing policies (simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation) + health checks. **ACM** issues free public TLS certs with auto-renewal (DNS validation); certificates for CloudFront must be in `us-east-1`.
questions.body_md:
Route 53: domains + DNS (public/private hosted zones), **alias records** to ALB/CloudFront (free, zone apex), routing policies (simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation) + health checks. **ACM** issues free public TLS certs with auto-renewal (DNS validation); certificates for CloudFront must be in `us-east-1`.

```
 app.example.com ─(Route 53 alias)─► CloudFront (ACM cert us-east-1) ─► ALB (ACM cert in region) ─► ECS
```

questions.title: EBS vs EFS vs S3
questions.short_md: EBS = block disk for one EC2 (AZ-scoped, snapshots). EFS = shared NFS file system across AZs/instances/tasks. S3 = object storage via API, unlimited, cheapest durable store.
questions.body_md: EBS = block disk for one EC2 (AZ-scoped, snapshots). EFS = shared NFS file system across AZs/instances/tasks. S3 = object storage via API, unlimited, cheapest durable store.

questions.title: SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge (vs Kinesis)
questions.short_md: **Common combos:** SNS → multiple SQS queues (fan-out with buffering); EventBridge rule → SQS → worker; S3 event → SQS → ECS worker.
questions.body_md:
| | **SQS** | **SNS** | **EventBridge** | Kinesis Data Streams |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pattern | queue (pull), point-to-point | pub/sub fan-out (push) | event bus with **content-based routing rules** | ordered stream, replay |
| Consumers | one consumer group processes each message | many subscribers | many targets per rule (20+ AWS targets), SaaS sources, schedules | multiple apps read same shard data |
| Buffering/retry | yes (visibility timeout, DLQ) | retries to endpoints, DLQ | retries, DLQ, **archive & replay** | retention up to 365 days |
| Ordering | FIFO queues | FIFO topics | no guarantee | per shard |

**Common combos:** SNS → multiple SQS queues (fan-out with buffering); EventBridge rule → SQS → worker; S3 event → SQS → ECS worker.

questions.title: SQS deep dive (frequently asked)
questions.short_md: - **Visibility timeout:** after a consumer receives a message, it's hidden for N seconds; if not deleted in time, it reappears (retry). Set > processing time; extend for long jobs. - **At-least-once delivery** (standard queues) → consumers must be **idempotent**. FIFO: exactly-once processing within dedup window + ordering per message group. - **DLQ** with `maxReceiveCount` for poison messages; redrive back after fixing. - **Long polling** (`WaitTimeSeconds=20`) reduces empty receives/cost. - Message size up to 1 MiB (store big payloads in S3, pass a pointer).
questions.body_md:
- **Visibility timeout:** after a consumer receives a message, it's hidden for N seconds; if not deleted in time, it reappears (retry). Set > processing time; extend for long jobs.

- **Long polling** (`WaitTimeSeconds=20`) reduces empty receives/cost.

questions.title: Idempotency in AWS integrations
questions.short_md: Because of retries and at-least-once delivery, the same request/event can arrive more than once. Make handlers safe to repeat: idempotency key (request ID, event ID) stored with a **conditional write** (DynamoDB `attribute_not_exists`), unique constraints, upserts, or AWS APIs' own client tokens (`ClientRequestToken`, `ClientToken`). Powertools for Lambda has an idempotency utility.

questions.title: Choreography with events vs orchestration
questions.short_md: EventBridge/SNS for loosely coupled reactions (choreography); **Step Functions** when you need a visible, controlled multi-step process with retries, timeouts and compensation (orchestration).

questions.title: CloudWatch vs CloudTrail vs X-Ray / OpenTelemetry
questions.short_md: fields @timestamp, level, request_id, msg
questions.body_md:
| Service | Answers |
|---|---|
| **CloudWatch Metrics & Alarms** | *how is it performing?* (latency, errors, CPU) → alarms → SNS/auto actions |
| **CloudWatch Logs** (+ Logs Insights queries) | *what did the app say?* |
| **CloudTrail** | *who called which AWS API, when, from where?* (audit, security) |
| **X-Ray / CloudWatch Application Signals / ADOT (OpenTelemetry)** | *where did the time go across services?* (distributed traces) |

```
fields @timestamp, level, request_id, msg
| filter level = "ERROR" and service = "api"
| stats count() by bin(5m)
```

questions.title: What to alarm on
questions.short_md: User-facing symptoms first (error rate, p99 latency, availability via synthetics), then saturation (CPU/memory, queue age, DB connections), and cost anomalies. Use composite alarms and SLO-based alerting to reduce noise.

questions.title: High availability across AZs
questions.short_md: Run ≥2 (ideally 3) AZs for every tier: ALB across AZs, ECS service spread across AZs, RDS Multi-AZ, NAT per AZ, stateless app instances, health checks + auto-replacement, avoid AZ-pinned single points (one NAT, one EC2). Test by simulating AZ failure (AWS Fault Injection Service).

Test by simulating AZ failure (AWS Fault Injection Service).

questions.title: Disaster recovery strategies
questions.short_md: **RTO** = how long to recover; **RPO** = how much data loss is acceptable. Tools: AWS Backup (cross-region copies), Aurora Global Database, DynamoDB global tables, S3 replication, Route 53 failover, IaC to rebuild. **Test DR regularly.**
questions.body_md:
| Strategy | RTO / RPO | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Backup & restore** | hours / hours | lowest |
| **Pilot light** (core data replicated, infra off) | tens of minutes | low |
| **Warm standby** (scaled-down copy running) | minutes | medium |
| **Multi-site active/active** | near zero | highest |

questions.title: Well-Architected Framework — 6 pillars
questions.short_md: **Operational excellence** (automate, observe, iterate) · **Security** (identity, least privilege, encryption, traceability) · **Reliability** (multi-AZ, recovery, quotas) · **Performance efficiency** (right services, measure) · **Cost optimisation** (right-size, pay for value, Graviton, Savings Plans) · **Sustainability** (efficient resource use). Lenses exist for serverless, generative AI, etc.

questions.title: Service quotas and throttling
questions.short_md: Most AWS APIs have rate limits and account quotas (Lambda concurrency, Bedrock tokens/min, ENIs). Design with backoff + jitter, request quota increases early, monitor `ThrottlingException`s, and spread load (queues).

questions.title: ECS task can't access S3 despite an IAM "Allow"
questions.short_md: Check in order: 1. **Which role?** The app uses the **task role**, not the execution role (execution role is for pulling images/logs). Is `taskRoleArn` set? Is the SDK actually using container credentials? 2. **Explicit deny** anywhere: SCP, permissions boundary, bucket policy (e.g., requires `aws:SourceVpce` or TLS), session policy. 3. **Resource ARN** correct (`arn:aws:s3:::bucket/*` for objects vs `arn:aws:s3:::bucket` for ListBucket). 4. **KMS:** object encrypted with a CMK — key policy must allow `kms:Decrypt` for the role. 5. **Network:** private subnet without NAT/S3 gateway endpoint → …
questions.body_md:
Check in order:
1. **Which role?** The app uses the **task role**, not the execution role (execution role is for pulling images/logs). Is `taskRoleArn` set? Is the SDK actually using container credentials?
2. **Explicit deny** anywhere: SCP, permissions boundary, bucket policy (e.g., requires `aws:SourceVpce` or TLS), session policy.
3. **Resource ARN** correct (`arn:aws:s3:::bucket/*` for objects vs `arn:aws:s3:::bucket` for ListBucket).
4. **KMS:** object encrypted with a CMK — key policy must allow `kms:Decrypt` for the role.
5. **Network:** private subnet without NAT/S3 gateway endpoint → timeout (not AccessDenied); endpoint policy may deny.
6. Cross-account bucket → bucket policy must also allow.
Tools: CloudTrail error event, IAM Policy Simulator, Access Analyzer.

questions.title: An internal API sometimes times out under load
questions.short_md: Measure where: ALB metrics (`TargetResponseTime`, 5xx, surge queue), ECS CPU/memory, app latency per dependency (traces), DB connections/CPU, NAT GW `ErrorPortAllocation`, DynamoDB/Bedrock throttling, Lambda concurrency. Typical fixes: connection pooling, autoscaling on right metric, timeouts + retries with backoff, caching, async processing via SQS, quota increases.

questions.title: "Connection timed out" vs "AccessDenied" — what does each tell you?
questions.short_md: **Timeout** = network path problem (SG, NACL, route table, missing NAT/endpoint, DNS to wrong IP). **AccessDenied** = network fine, IAM/resource policy problem. **Connection refused** = reached host but nothing listening on that port.
questions.body_md: **Timeout** = network path problem (SG, NACL, route table, missing NAT/endpoint, DNS to wrong IP). **AccessDenied** = network fine, IAM/resource policy problem. **Connection refused** = reached host but nothing listening on that port.

questions.title: Design secure cross-account access for a central agent platform calling team accounts
questions.short_md: Central account role → assumes per-team roles (`sts:AssumeRole`) with trust limited to the platform role ARN + `aws:PrincipalOrgID`; team roles grant only specific tools' actions; session tags carry end-user/tenant for ABAC; CloudTrail in both accounts; SCPs prevent privilege escalation.

questions.title: How do you present an AWS design trade-off in an interview?
questions.short_md: Structure: requirements (latency, scale, compliance) → 2 options → compare on **security, reliability, cost, operability, performance** → choose with reasoning → risks + mitigations → how you'd validate (load test, cost estimate). Example: "API Gateway + Lambda vs ALB + ECS for an agent API: streaming for minutes and steady load favour ALB + ECS; spiky low traffic favours Lambda."

sections.title: Cheat sheet
sections.intro_md:
| Topic | Remember |
|---|---|
| Region/AZ | ≥2 AZs for HA; region by latency/compliance |
| Public subnet | route 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW |
| NAT GW | outbound only for private; per-GB cost; one per AZ |
| SG vs NACL | stateful/ENI/allow-only vs stateless/subnet/allow+deny |
| Endpoints | gateway (S3, DynamoDB, free) vs interface (PrivateLink) |
| IAM eval | explicit deny > guardrails (SCP/boundary) > allow > default deny |
| Cross-account | caller policy AND resource policy |
| Roles | temporary creds; task role ≠ execution role |
| KMS | envelope encryption; key policy controls use |
| ALB vs NLB | L7 routing vs L4 performance/static IP |
| API GW vs ALB | per-request, auth/throttle, ~29 s vs long-lived/streaming |
| SQS | at-least-once, visibility timeout, DLQ, idempotent consumers |
| SNS / EventBridge | fan-out / content routing + replay |
| Observability | metrics (how much), logs (what), traces (where), CloudTrail (who) |
| DR | backup-restore → pilot light → warm standby → active/active |
